ai.literal: Than poverty that which is painful what if one asks, than poverty poverty itself is that which is painful.
ai.translation: If one asks what is as painful as poverty, the answer is that nothing is as painful as poverty itself.
ai.modern: வறுமையை விடக் கொடுமையானது எது என்று கேட்டால், வறுமையை விட வறுமையே கொடுமையானது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the incomparable suffering of poverty. The poet poses a rhetorical question asking what could possibly be more painful than being poor. By answering that only poverty itself is as painful as poverty, the verse emphasizes that no other misery in the world can match its devastating nature. The repetition of the words for poverty and pain reinforces the absolute and inescapable grip of destitution.

ai.literal: Poverty called a sinner, next life and this life without, will come.
ai.translation: The wretched sinner called poverty comes, depriving a person of the blessings of both this life and the next.
ai.modern: வறுமை என்று சொல்லப்படும் ஒரு பாவி, ஒருவருக்கு இப்பிறப்பின் இன்பத்தையும் மறுபிறப்பின் இன்பத்தையும் இல்லாமல் செய்து வந்து சேரும்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, poverty is personified as a wretched sinner ('பாவி'). The author explains that when poverty comes, it completely strips a person of the joys and virtues of both this present life ('இம்மை') and the next life ('மறுமை'). In this world, a poor person lacks the means to live with dignity and comfort, and because they cannot afford to perform acts of charity, they are also deprived of merit for the next world. Thus, poverty is depicted as an all-consuming affliction that ruins a person's existence across both realms.

ai.literal: Ancient lineage and dignity will destroy completely, the craving called poverty.
ai.translation: The craving called poverty will completely destroy both one's ancient lineage and dignity.
ai.modern: வறுமை என்று சொல்லப்படும் பேராசை, ஒருவருடைய பழமையான குடிப்பெருமையையும் அவரது நற்பண்புகளையும் ஒருசேர அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the destructive nature of poverty by describing it as a 'craving' (நசை), because extreme want forces a person to beg and desire things constantly. This desperate state of poverty completely (தொகையாக) ruins two of a person's most valuable possessions: their ancient family lineage (தொல்வரவு) and their personal dignity or lustre (தோல்). The word 'தோல்' here refers to the natural dignity, beauty, or self-respect of an individual, which is lost when one is reduced to begging. The term 'தொகையாக' emphasizes that these noble qualities are not lost gradually, but are wiped out all at once by the onset of poverty.

ai.literal: Even in those born of noble family, poverty will bring a weariness that causes humiliating words to arise.
ai.translation: Even in those born of noble birth, poverty brings a weariness of mind that gives rise to degrading words.
ai.modern: உயர்ந்த குடியில் பிறந்தவர்களிடத்திலும், வறுமையானது இழிவான சொற்கள் தோன்றுவதற்குக் காரணமான சோர்வினை உண்டாக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the devastating psychological impact of poverty. Even individuals born into noble families, who are naturally refined in speech and conduct, are not immune to its effects. Poverty causes a deep mental weariness or lapse in self-control (cōrvu). This exhaustion weakens their resolve, leading them to utter humiliating or begging words (iḷivanda col) that they would otherwise never speak.

ai.literal: Within the affliction called poverty, many kinds of sufferings going into will occur.
ai.translation: Within the single affliction known as poverty, countless other diverse sufferings will enter and take root.
ai.modern: வறுமை என்று சொல்லப்படும் துன்பத்திற்குள், பல வகையான துன்பங்கள் சென்று சேரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that poverty is not just a single hardship, but a source of multiple miseries. The word 'iṭumpai' means affliction, and 'iṭumpaiyuḷ' indicates that within the state of poverty, other troubles reside. The term 'palkurai' refers to many different kinds or varieties. Thus, once a person falls into poverty, various other forms of suffering—such as hunger, loss of respect, and helplessness—will naturally enter and afflict them.

ai.literal: A noble subject well having understood even if they speak, of those who are poor, the meaning of the words decline will suffer.
ai.translation: Even if the poor speak with a deep and thorough understanding of a noble subject, the meaning of their words will lose its value.
ai.modern: வறுமையுற்றவர் ஒரு நல்ல கருத்தை நன்கு ஆராய்ந்து உணர்ந்து சொன்னாலும், அவருடைய சொற்களின் பொருள் மதிப்பற்றதாகிப் போகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the harsh social reality of poverty, where a person's financial status dictates how their intellect is received. Even if a poor person speaks on a noble and valuable subject with profound understanding, society fails to appreciate it. The words they utter lose their weight and value simply because of the speaker's impoverished state. Thus, poverty robs a person not just of material wealth, but also of the intellectual respect they deserve.

ai.literal: Virtue-not-associating poverty, the mother who bore [him] even, like a stranger, to be looked at will happen.
ai.translation: Even the mother who gave birth to him will look upon a man as a stranger, if he is afflicted by poverty that is devoid of virtue.
ai.modern: அறநெறியோடு பொருந்தாத வறுமை உடையவனை, அவனைப் பெற்ற தாயும் கூட ஒரு அந்நியனைப் போலத் தான் பார்ப்பாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the devastating social impact of poverty. The poet states that when a person is trapped in a miserable poverty that lacks any virtuous support or dignity, even their own mother will look at them coldly, as if they were a stranger. The term 'அறஞ்சாரா' (not aligned with virtue) suggests a state of destitution so severe that it strips away moral standing and social respect. By using the mother—the ultimate symbol of unconditional love—as the one who turns away, the verse emphasizes how poverty destroys even the strongest human bonds.

ai.literal: Even today, will it come? - that poverty which, even yesterday, killed me as it were.
ai.translation: Will poverty, which felt as though it killed me even yesterday, come to torment me today as well?
ai.modern: நேற்றும் என்னைக் கொன்றது போலத் துன்புறுத்திய வறுமை, இன்றும் என்னிடம் வருமோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet vividly portrays the relentless, daily agony of extreme poverty. The speaker expresses dread, wondering if poverty—which inflicted such severe suffering yesterday that it felt like death—will return to torment them again today. By comparing the daily struggle of destitution to being killed repeatedly, the poet emphasizes that poverty is not a one-time hardship but a continuous, exhausting battle for survival.

words.gloss: closing of the eyes in sleep

ai.literal: Inside fire sleeping even is possible; in poverty any one closing of eyes is difficult.
ai.translation: It is possible even to sleep while enveloped in fire; but in the midst of poverty, it is impossible to get even a wink of sleep.
ai.modern: நெருப்புக்குள் படுத்துத் தூங்குவதும் கூடச் சாத்தியமாகும்; ஆனால் வறுமையின் துன்பத்தில் வாழும்போது சிறிதும் கண்மூடித் தூங்குவது என்பது முடியாததாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts physical torment with the mental agony of destitution. The poet states that one might somehow manage to fall asleep even when surrounded by burning fire, but it is absolutely impossible to find any sleep when trapped in extreme poverty. The word 'நிரப்பு' specifically denotes poverty or emptiness, and 'கண்பாடு' refers to the closing of eyes to sleep. Through this extreme comparison, the verse highlights how the constant worry and anxiety of poverty are far more sleepless and agonizing than physical heat.

ai.literal: Those who lack basic resources, completely not renouncing, is death to salt and to sour gruel.
ai.translation: For those who lack the basic resources of life, not renouncing domestic life completely is a death-blow to even their meager salt and sour gruel.
ai.modern: அனுபவிக்கத்தக்க பொருள்கள் இல்லாதவர்கள், இல்லற வாழ்க்கையை முற்றிலும் துறந்துவிடாமல் இருப்பது, அவர்கள் உண்ணும் எளிய உப்பிற்கும் கஞ்சிக்கும் கூட எமனாக (அழிவாக) முடியும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the extreme misery of poverty in domestic life. The word 'துப்புரவு' refers to the basic resources or comforts of life, while 'துவர' means completely. When destitute people who lack even basic amenities refuse to completely renounce the householder's life, they struggle to survive. Their desperate attempt to maintain a household makes them consume even the cheapest, most basic food items like salt and sour gruel, thereby acting as a destroyer to these meager provisions. The poet uses the image of 'death' to show how poverty reduces a person to a state where even the simplest sustenance is exhausted.
